feedback: If the learner loses track of the tilt direction while rotating the view, pause and trace the axis arrow — it points the same way regardless of your viewpoint.
Confirm that the pole tilted toward the Sun has summer and endless daylight, and the pole tilted away has winter and endless night.
activities.intendedInsight: Earth-Sun geometry is genuinely three-dimensional; viewing the tilt from different angles can build spatial intuition for why one pole is bathed in light while the other is in darkness.
learnerActions: Move your viewpoint around a 3D Earth-Sun orbit to look at the tilted axis from different angles.

At each of four orbital positions, identify which pole is leaning toward the Sun and which is leaning away. Notice that at the two in-between (equinox) positions, neither pole leans toward the Sun, and both poles get some day and some night.
At the two positions where one pole leans fully toward the Sun, describe how the lit pole experiences continuous daylight and the dark pole continuous night.
activities.title: Fly around the orbit in 3D to find the sunward-leaning pole

feedback: If a learner tips the globe to point at the torch each time, stop and reset: the axis must keep pointing the same direction; only your position around the torch changes.
Confirm that the pole in continuous light is having summer and the pole in continuous shadow is having winter.
activities.intendedInsight: A pole tilted toward the light source stays lit even as Earth spins, giving continuous daylight; a pole tilted away stays dark, giving continuous night.
learnerActions: Tilt a globe so its axis points a fixed direction, then carry it around a torch standing in for the Sun, keeping the tilt pointing the same way the whole time.
Spin the globe at the position where one pole leans toward the torch and watch that pole stay in the light through a full spin (midnight sun).
Carry the globe to the opposite side and spin it again to see that pole stay in shadow (polar night).
Describe what season each pole is having at each position.
activities.title: Torch-and-tilted-globe demonstration

feedback: If a learner picks 'closer in summer', counter with simultaneity: when the north has summer the south has winter though both are at similar distance from the Sun — so it must be the tilt.
If a learner says the Sun is just brighter/hotter in summer, note the Sun's output is steady; what changes is how directly and how long its light reaches a place, because of the tilt.
Credit answers that link the tilt to sea ice growing in winter and shrinking in summer, or to animals migrating and breeding on the seasonal cycle.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner who understands credits the axial tilt (not distance) and can connect the seasonal cycle to at least one consequence such as sea-ice change or animal behaviour.
learnerActions: Answer which-pole-has-summer questions for given orbital positions.
Decide whether tilt or distance explains the seasons, using the fact that opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same time.
Explain how the same tilt links to sea ice spreading in winter and shrinking in summer, and to animal migration or breeding on the yearly cycle.
activities.title: Check understanding: tilt vs distance and which pole has summer
